stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A county hydrologist selected 50 wells at random from the 1,200 private wells registered in the county and tested water from each one. Water from 18 of the 50 sampled wells had a nitrate level above the state drinking-water limit.

I. Exactly 36% of the 1,200 registered wells in the county have nitrate levels above the state limit.
II. Of the 50 sampled wells, 32 had nitrate levels that were not above the state limit.
explanation: Statement II is only about the 50 wells that were tested. If 18 of them were above the limit, then $50 - 18 = 32$ were not, so II must be true. Statement I takes the sample rate, $\frac{18}{50} = 36\%$, and claims it is the exact rate for all 1,200 wells. A random sample gives you a reasonable estimate of the county rate, but it does not guarantee that value, so I does not have to be true.

A.why: You treated the 36% from the random sample as the exact rate for all 1,200 wells. Random selection makes 36% a reasonable estimate, not a guaranteed value. You also passed over statement II, which is a plain fact about the sampled wells.

C.why: You were right about II, but you also accepted I. The sample's 36% does not have to match the county's exact rate. The true rate could easily be a little higher or lower.

D.why: You rejected every statement because it mentioned a number. Statement II is limited to the 50 sampled wells, and the data fix that count at $50 - 18 = 32$, so it must be true.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A mapping agency's digital database contains 2,000 street names. A cartographer checked a random sample of 80 of these names against official records and found that 6 of the 80 were misspelled.

I. If the cartographer checked a different random sample of 80 street names from the database, exactly 6 of them would be misspelled.
II. Exactly 150 of the 2,000 street names in the database are misspelled.
explanation: The sample rate is $\frac{6}{80} = 7.5\%$, and $7.5\%$ of 2,000 is 150. Statement II says the database contains exactly that many misspellings. A sample only estimates the database rate, so II does not have to be true. Statement I is also wrong because a second random sample will usually give a somewhat different count. Neither statement must be true.

A.why: You assumed a second random sample would give the identical result. Each random sample varies, so a new group of 80 names could easily have 4, 7 or 9 misspellings.

B.why: You calculated $7.5\%$ of 2,000 correctly and got 150. But you treated that figure as the exact count for the whole database. It is an estimate, not a value the sample guarantees.

C.why: You accepted both claims of exactness. A random sample does not lock in the result of another sample, and it does not lock in the population count either.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
An agricultural research farm is divided into 600 plots. A soil scientist selected 40 of the plots at random and measured the soil pH of each one. The mean pH of the 40 sampled plots was 6.4.

I. The mean soil pH of all 600 plots on the farm is 6.4.
II. The mean soil pH of the plots on a neighboring farm is 6.4.
III. The value 6.4 is an estimate of the mean soil pH of all 600 plots on the farm.
explanation: The 40 plots were chosen at random from this farm's 600 plots, so their mean of 6.4 is a reasonable estimate of the mean for all 600 plots. That is exactly what III says. Statement I claims the farm-wide mean equals 6.4 exactly, which the sample cannot guarantee. Statement II applies the result to a different farm that was never sampled.

A.why: You treated the sample mean as the exact mean for all 600 plots. A random sample estimates the population mean but does not pin it down. You also passed over III, which is the correctly hedged statement.

C.why: You were right about III, but you also accepted I. The word "estimate" in III is what makes it true, and statement I drops that hedge by claiming the exact value.

D.why: You applied the sample result to a neighboring farm. The plots were drawn only from this farm, so the data say nothing about soil anywhere else.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A city has 24,000 adult residents. Its planning department surveyed a random sample of 300 of them about a proposed protected bike lane on Harbor Avenue, and 45% of the residents surveyed said they favored the bike lane.

I. If the department surveyed another random sample of 300 adult residents of the city, exactly 45% of them would favor the bike lane.
II. Exactly 10,800 adult residents of the city favor the bike lane.
explanation: Statement II turns the sample percentage into a citywide count: $0.45 \times 24{,}000 = 10{,}800$. Then it claims that count is exact, but 45% is only an estimate of the citywide share, so II does not have to be true. Statement I says a new random sample would give the identical 45%, and sample results vary from one sample to the next. Neither statement must be true.

B.why: You assumed a repeat survey would give exactly the same percentage. Two random samples of 300 residents will almost always give slightly different results.

C.why: Your arithmetic was right, since $0.45 \times 24{,}000 = 10{,}800$. But you treated that number as the exact count for the city. The sample only lets you estimate the citywide figure.

D.why: You accepted both claims of exactness. The word "must" rules out both, because a random sample makes an estimate reasonable but never guarantees it.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
At an excavation site, archaeologists have catalogued 900 pottery fragments. A researcher selected 60 of the catalogued fragments at random and found that 15 of the 60 had painted decoration.

I. Of the sampled fragments, 25% had painted decoration.
II. Exactly 225 of the 900 catalogued fragments have painted decoration.
III. At a nearby excavation site, 25% of the pottery fragments have painted decoration.
explanation: Statement I only describes the sample: $\frac{15}{60} = 25\%$, so it must be true. Statement II applies that rate to all 900 fragments ($0.25 \times 900 = 225$) and claims the count is exact, which a sample cannot guarantee. Statement III carries the result to a different site that was never sampled. Only I must be true.

A.why: You took the population count you calculated from the sample rate and treated it as exact. You also left out I, which is a direct fact about the 60 fragments the researcher examined.

B.why: You were right about I, but you also accepted II. The sample rate of 25% estimates the rate for all 900 fragments, so the true count could be somewhat more or less than 225.

D.why: You applied the sample to a different site. The fragments were drawn only from this site's catalogue, so the result does not carry over to a nearby excavation.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
In a vaccine trial, 3,000 volunteers received the vaccine. Immunologists selected 120 of these volunteers at random and measured the antibody concentration in each one's blood four weeks after vaccination. The mean concentration for the 120 volunteers was 48 units per milliliter.

I. The mean antibody concentration four weeks after vaccination for all 3,000 vaccinated volunteers is 48 units per milliliter.
II. If the immunologists selected another random sample of 120 of the 3,000 vaccinated volunteers, the mean antibody concentration four weeks after vaccination would be 48 units per milliliter.
explanation: The sample mean of 48 units per milliliter is a reasonable estimate of the mean for all 3,000 vaccinated volunteers, but it is not guaranteed to equal that mean, so I does not have to be true. A different random sample of 120 volunteers would very likely give a somewhat different mean, so II does not have to be true either.

A.why: You treated the sample mean as the exact mean for all 3,000 volunteers. Random selection makes 48 a reasonable estimate, not a guaranteed value.

B.why: You assumed a repeat sample would reproduce the same mean. Individual antibody levels vary, so a new group of 120 volunteers would almost certainly give a slightly different mean.

D.why: You accepted both statements. Neither the population mean nor a second sample's mean has to equal the value from this one sample.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A sky survey catalogued 10,000 stars in one region of the sky. Astronomers selected 250 of the catalogued stars at random and studied each one closely. They found that 40 of the 250 stars belong to binary star systems.

I. Exactly 1,600 of the 10,000 catalogued stars belong to binary star systems.
II. The sample proportion, 16%, is an estimate of the proportion of catalogued stars in the region that belong to binary star systems.
explanation: The sample proportion is $\frac{40}{250} = 16\%$. The 250 stars were chosen at random from the catalogue, so 16% is a reasonable estimate of the proportion for all 10,000 catalogued stars, and II must be true. Statement I uses $0.16 \times 10{,}000 = 1{,}600$ and claims that count is exact, which a sample cannot guarantee.

A.why: You were right about II, but you also accepted I. Turning the sample rate into a count of 1,600 is fine as an estimate, but the word "exactly" makes the claim go beyond what the sample shows.

B.why: You rejected II as if it claimed an exact value. Statement II only calls 16% an estimate, and a random sample does support that. Notice the hedge before you rule a statement out.

C.why: You treated the count from the sample rate, $0.16 \times 10{,}000 = 1{,}600$, as the exact number of binary stars. You also rejected II, which is the correctly hedged statement.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
Marine biologists have attached tracking tags to 1,500 green sea turtles in a coastal feeding area. The biologists selected 45 of the tagged turtles at random and measured each turtle's shell length. The mean shell length of the 45 turtles was 82 centimeters.

I. The mean shell length of all 1,500 tagged green sea turtles is 82 centimeters.
II. The mean shell length of the untagged green sea turtles in the same feeding area is 82 centimeters.
explanation: The 45 turtles were chosen at random from the 1,500 tagged turtles, so their mean of 82 centimeters is a reasonable estimate of the mean for all tagged turtles. It is not guaranteed to be the exact mean, so I does not have to be true. Statement II applies the result to the untagged turtles, which were never part of the population sampled. Neither statement must be true.

B.why: You treated the sample mean as the exact mean for all 1,500 tagged turtles. Random selection makes 82 cm a reasonable estimate of that mean, not a guaranteed value.

C.why: You applied the sample to the untagged turtles. The sample was drawn only from tagged turtles, so the result does not tell you about a group that was never sampled.

D.why: You accepted both statements. The sample cannot guarantee the exact mean for tagged turtles, and it says nothing about untagged ones.
